benchmark_item.question: My corgi runs through the snow straight at the camera. Is he excited?

answer.question: My corgi runs through the snow straight at the camera. Is he excited?

behaviors_seen.description: turning in tight circles (after its own tail or not)
rhythmic bobbing, nodding or rotating of the head while awake

explained_behaviors.summary: Turning in tight circles after the tail. Common, and usually brief; in some dogs it is habitual and hard to interrupt.
explained_behaviors.temporal_notes: A bout is repeated whole-body turning in place; the number of turns, how long bouts last and whether they recur matter more than a single turn.

play_or_normal.explanation: self-directed play or excitement, especially in young dogs, when bouts are brief and the dog is easy to distract

request.explanation: a learned way to get attention: owners often laugh at or encourage tail chasing, which can reinforce it; some dogs start when nobody attends to them

arousal_or_stress.explanation: frustration or arousal in a waiting or conflict situation (for example waiting for food, or when the owner talks to other people)

compulsive.explanation: canine compulsive disorder: habitual, perseverative chasing with lowered responsiveness, often with other repetitive behaviours (light chasing, freezing); more common in some breeds (bull terriers, German shepherds)

medical.explanation: a physical cause near the tail or a neurological one: tail or anal-sac discomfort, skin itch, pain, or focal seizures; behaviour and medical causes can coexist

circling that is not tail chasing: tight circles always in the same direction, often with a head tilt or head turn, loss of balance or episodes that cannot be interrupted, point to a balance (vestibular) or brain problem

explained_behaviors.summary: Rhythmic bobbing, nodding or rotating of the head while the dog is awake.

medical.explanation: shaking the head to the side because of ear discomfort is a different movement (a vigorous shake, often with ear scratching)

idiopathic head tremor: episodes of head bobbing in an alert dog that usually stop when the dog is distracted (called, offered food or a toy); considered benign but diagnosed after other causes are excluded
a focal seizure, the main alternative: it is not stopped by distraction and may come with drooling, unresponsiveness or other signs

explained_behaviors.no_request_note: No request or intention is implied by this behaviour itself.

uncertainty: The recording can show what the animal does and when; it cannot establish why. Candidate explanations come from the cited sources, ordered by how well your description matches them.
Behaviour recognition uses a general vision-language model (zero-shot); scores are relative, not probabilities, and its measured accuracy is in results/e31.
No usable sound in the recording, so vocalizations could not be checked.
Context taken from the recording (people, objects, sounds, place) comes from automatic detectors and can be wrong; it changes the order of the candidates only half as much as your description.
observations_needed: How old was the dog when it started, and how often does it happen (occasionally or daily)?
Can you interrupt it by calling the dog or offering a toy, and does it respond to you during a bout?
In which situations does it start (waiting for food, when people talk to each other, when left alone, when excited)?
Does the dog bite or injure the tail, scoot, or show hair loss or sores near the tail base?
Are there other repetitive behaviours such as chasing lights or shadows, snapping at the air, freezing or staring?
Does it always circle in the same direction, with a head tilt or loss of balance, even without looking at its tail?
Does the dog stay alert, and does the movement stop when you call it or offer a treat?
Is it a small rhythmic bobbing (yes-yes, no-no) or a vigorous shake as if shaking off water or an ear problem?
urgent_signs: the tail is wounded or bleeding
bouts cannot be interrupted or interfere with eating or sleeping
episodes with staring, unresponsiveness or snapping at the air (possible seizures)
circling with a head tilt, falling or loss of balance
episodes with unresponsiveness, drooling, collapse or loss of bladder control
a first episode in an older dog

sources.citation: Burn CC (2011) A vicious cycle: a cross-sectional study of canine tail-chasing and human responses to it, using a free video-sharing website. PLoS ONE 6(11): e26553.
sources.supports: 400 online videos: about a third of tail-chasing dogs chased habitually or were hard to distract; perseverative dogs showed fewer play behaviours; laughter in 55 % and encouragement in 43 % of videos, so owner attention may reinforce it

sources.citation: Tiira K et al. (2012) Environmental effects on compulsive tail chasing in dogs. PLoS ONE 7(7): e41684.
sources.supports: questionnaire study of 368 dogs: early onset (3-6 months), lowered responsiveness during bouts in about half of tail chasers, co-occurring compulsions; supplementary videos describe chasing when waiting for food, when the owner talks to others, or when nobody pays attention

sources.citation: Van Haevermaet et al. (2026) Tail chasing in a dog: false dichotomy between behavioural and medical problems. Veterinary Record Case Reports.
sources.supports: tail chasing can combine behavioural and medical causes

sources.citation: Behavioral and autonomic manifestations of suspected focal impaired awareness seizures supported by interictal EEG (three dogs). Front Vet Sci (2026).
sources.supports: fly-catching, air snapping, staring and lip licking with impaired awareness can be focal seizures mistaken for behavioural disorders

sources.citation: Merck Veterinary Manual: The neurologic examination of animals.
sources.supports: a head tilt usually indicates vestibular dysfunction; animals with forebrain lesions may turn their heads and circle in one direction

sources.citation: dvm360: Vestibular disease in dogs and cats (proceedings).
sources.supports: vestibular disorders cause head tilt, falling, rolling, leaning, circling and abnormal eye movements; circling also occurs with focal forebrain lesions

sources.citation: Veterinary Partner (VIN): Vestibular disease in dogs and cats.
sources.supports: middle- and inner-ear problems are separate from brain problems; localizing the cause decides outlook and treatment
most dogs (up to 87 %) can be distracted out of an episode; the dog stays alert; the primary differential is focal seizure activity, which distraction does not stop and which may show autonomic signs

answer.summary: In the recording: turning in tight circles (after its own tail or not) (0.0-18.0 s); rhythmic bobbing, nodding or rotating of the head while awake (2.5-3.0 s, 5.5-6.0 s, 9.0-9.5 s). Movement: the animal stays roughly in place while moving. Turning in tight circles (after its own tail or not) (recording) has several possible explanations, in order of fit to your description: ordinary play or maintenance behaviour; a request or intention directed at a person; arousal, frustration or stress; an abnormal repetitive (compulsive) pattern; discomfort, itch, pain or a neurological cause. Rhythmic bobbing, nodding or rotating of the head while awake (recording) is usually discomfort, itch, pain or a neurological cause. No request is implied by it. The cause is not established from the recording; the questions listed would help tell the candidates apart.
